The story strikes a strong and effective balance between scene and summary/exposition. It opens with brief exposition to establish Arthur's age, profession, and the setting, quickly transitioning into a vivid, real-time scene as he discovers the car crash and scrambles down the slope. During the "two to four hours" he waits for help, the writer skillfully alternates between compressed summaries of passing time (the shadow crossing the ridge, the cold coming up, the dark settling in) and immediate, dramatized scenes of Arthur speaking aloud to the deceased woman and observing the details of the wreck. Furthermore, much of the character exposition—such as his memories of his first boss, his father's hardware store, and his ended marriage—is woven seamlessly into the scene via his one-sided dialogue, keeping the narrative emotionally engaging while still delivering necessary background information and maintaining a steady, contemplative pace.
